nodes.name: Fixed-point subgroup H and generalized symmetric space Q
nodes.statement_short: For an automorphism $\theta$ of finite order, $H$ is the set of $\theta$-fixed points and $Q$ the set of elements $x\theta(x)^{-1}$.

nodes.name: Generalized Symmetric Space
nodes.statement: The set $H$ is the fixed-point subgroup of $\theta$ and $Q$ is known as a {\em Generalized Symmetric Space}.

nodes.name: theta-twisted conjugation
nodes.statement:
Both $G$ and $H$ act on $Q$ by $\theta$-twisted conjugation which we denote by $*$. For $g\in G$ and $q\in Q$ we have
$$g*q=gq\theta(g)^{-1}.$$

nodes.name: Q is isomorphic to G/H for involutions
nodes.statement: Also, if $\theta$ is an involution, then $Q\cong G/H$ under the map $\tau : G\to Q$ given by $\tau(g)=g\theta(g)^{-1}$.
conclusions: $Q\cong G/H$ under the map $\tau : G\to Q$ given by $\tau(g)=g\theta(g)^{-1}$

nodes.name: H-orbits on Q correspond to H-double cosets
nodes.statement: In particular, if $\theta$ is an involution it is known that $H\backslash Q\cong H\backslash G/H$.
conclusions: $H\backslash Q\cong H\backslash G/H$

nodes.name: Dihedral group D_n
nodes.statement:
Throughout the paper we denote by $D_n$ the group of symmetries of the
regular $n$-gon. More specifically, $D_n$ is a finitely generated
group given by the presentation
$$D_n=\langle r,s\mid r^n=s^2=1,\ sr=r^{-1}s\rangle.$$
nodes.section: 1.1 The Dihedral Group and its Automorphism Group

nodes.name: Normal form in D_n
nodes.statement:
From the presentation it is clear
that
\[ D_n = \{ 1, r, r^2, \ldots, r^{n-1}, s, rs, r^2s, \ldots, r^{n-1}s
\} \]
and we say that an element of $D_n$ is presented in \emph{normal form}
if it is written as $r^ks^m$ for some integers $0 \le k < n$ and $s
\in \{0, 1\}$.
nodes.section: 1.1 The Dihedral Group and its Automorphism Group
nodes.statement_short: Every element of $D_n$ is written uniquely as $r^ks^m$ with $0\le k<n$, $m\in\{0,1\}$ (normal form).

nodes.name: Z_n and the unit group U_n
nodes.statement:
Throughout the paper, $\mathbb{Z}_n$ denotes the additive group of integers
modulo $n$ and $U_n$ denotes the multiplicative group of units of
$\mathbb{Z}_n$.
nodes.section: 1.1 The Dihedral Group and its Automorphism Group

nodes.name: k-th roots of unity R_n^k
nodes.statement:
We also find it useful to have terminology for the $k$-th roots of unity in $\mathbb{Z}_n$ (equivalently in $U_n$), which can be described by
$$\mathcal{R}_n^k:=\{a\in U_n\mid a^k=1\}.$$
nodes.section: 1.1 The Dihedral Group and its Automorphism Group

nodes.name: Automorphism group of D_n is Aff(Z_n)
nodes.statement:
The automorphism group of $D_n$ is isomorphic to the 
group of affine linear transformations of $\mathbb{Z}_n$:
$$\operatorname{Aut}(D_n)\cong \operatorname{Aff}(\mathbb{Z}_n)=\left\{ ax+b: \mathbb{Z}_n\to\mathbb{Z}_n \mid a \in U_n, b \in
\mathbb{Z}_n \right\}$$
and the action of $ax+b$ on elements of $D_n$ in normal form is given by:
\[ (ax+b).(r^k s^m) = r^{ak+bm}s^m.\]
nodes.section: 1.1 The Dihedral Group and its Automorphism Group
conclusions:
The automorphism group of $D_n$ is isomorphic to the 
group of affine linear transformations of $\mathbb{Z}_n$

the action of $ax+b$ on elements of $D_n$ in normal form is given by:
\[ (ax+b).(r^k s^m) = r^{ak+bm}s^m.\]
nodes.statement_short: $\operatorname{Aut}(D_n)\cong\operatorname{Aff}(\mathbb{Z}_n)$, with $ax+b$ sending $r^ks^m$ to $r^{ak+bm}s^m$.
nodes.label: lem:aut

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 1.1
nodes.statement:
Observe that $\theta(r)$ must have order $n$ since $r$ does. The
elements of $D_n$ of order $n$ are precisely the $\{ r^a \mid a \in
U_n \}$.
So let $\theta(r) = r^a$ for some $a$ relatively prime to
$n$. Similarly, $\theta(s)=r^bs$ for some $0 \le b < n$ since $s$ has
order 2 and the only elements of $D_n$ of order 2 are of the form $r^bs$.
Putting these together, we see that if
$\theta\in\operatorname{Aut}(D_n)$, then for any $r^ks^m\in D_n$ we must have
$\theta(r^ks^m)=r^{ak+bm}s^m$. There is now a clear map from
$\operatorname{Aut}(D_n)\to \operatorname{Aff}(\mathbb{Z}_n)$ and it is easily checked to be an isomorphism.
nodes.section: 1.1 The Dihedral Group and its Automorphism Group
nodes.statement_short: Determine the possible images of the generators $r$ (order $n$) and $s$ (order 2), giving the affine map $r^ks^m\mapsto r^{ak+bm}s^m$.

nodes.name: Images of generators
nodes.statement:
Observe that $\theta(r)$ must have order $n$ since $r$ does. The
elements of $D_n$ of order $n$ are precisely the $\{ r^a \mid a \in
U_n \}$.
So let $\theta(r) = r^a$ for some $a$ relatively prime to
$n$. Similarly, $\theta(s)=r^bs$ for some $0 \le b < n$ since $s$ has
order 2 and the only elements of $D_n$ of order 2 are of the form $r^bs$.
nodes.section: 1.1 The Dihedral Group and its Automorphism Group
nodes.statement_short: $\theta(r)=r^a$ with $a$ a unit and $\theta(s)=r^bs$ by order considerations.

nodes.name: Affine formula and isomorphism
nodes.statement:
Putting these together, we see that if
$\theta\in\operatorname{Aut}(D_n)$, then for any $r^ks^m\in D_n$ we must have
$\theta(r^ks^m)=r^{ak+bm}s^m$. There is now a clear map from
$\operatorname{Aut}(D_n)\to \operatorname{Aff}(\mathbb{Z}_n)$ and it is easily checked to be an isomorphism.
nodes.section: 1.1 The Dihedral Group and its Automorphism Group
nodes.statement_short: Combine to get $\theta(r^ks^m)=r^{ak+bm}s^m$ and the isomorphism to $\operatorname{Aff}(\mathbb{Z}_n)$.

nodes.name: Notation theta = ax+b
nodes.statement:
Throughout the paper we abuse notation and write $\theta = ax+b$ for
elements $\theta \in \operatorname{Aut}(D_n)$ according to Lemma \ref{lem:aut}.
nodes.section: 1.1 The Dihedral Group and its Automorphism Group

nodes.name: Inner automorphisms of D_n
nodes.statement:
Consider $\theta = \operatorname{conj}(g)$,
  conjugation by an element $g\in D_n$. 
  If $\theta = ax + b$ from Lemma \ref{lem:aut}, and
  if $g=r^k$, then it is easy to see that $a=1$ and
  $b=2k$ (in $U_n$ and $\mathbb{Z}_n$ respectively). Also, if $g=r^ks$, then we have $a=n-1$ and
  $b=2k$. In particular, if $\theta=ax+b$ is an \emph{inner automorphism},
  then (abusing notation) we have $a\equiv\pm 1 \pmod{n}$. Also, we see that when $n$ is even, there are $n$
  distinct inner automorphisms (corresponding to $a\equiv\pm 1\pmod{n}$ and $b\in\langle2\rangle\leq
  \mathbb{Z}_n$, and when $n$ is odd, there are $2n$ distinct inner automorphisms
  corresponding to $a\equiv\pm 1\pmod{n}$ and $b\in\langle2\rangle=\mathbb{Z}_n$.  Finally, note
  that the identity automorphism of $D_n$
  corresponds to $x \in \operatorname{Aff}(\mathbb{Z}_n)$.
nodes.section: 1.1 The Dihedral Group and its Automorphism Group
nodes.statement_short: Conjugation by $r^k$ is $x+2k$, by $r^ks$ is $(n-1)x+2k$; inner automorphisms have $a\equiv\pm1$, numbering $n$ or $2n$ by parity of $n$.

nodes.name: Diagram automorphism
nodes.statement:
It is well known from the theory of Coxeter groups that when $n$ is
  even, there is an outer automorphism of $D_n$ corresponding to the
  interchanging of the two conjugacy classes of reflections, also
  known as the diagram automorphism (cf. \cite[\S4.2]{Bourbaki}). This
  automorphism is described by $\theta=ax+b$ where $a=n-1$ and
  $b=n-1$. The previous example shows that this automorphism
  is inner when $n$ is odd, and outer when $n$ is even.
nodes.section: 1.1 The Dihedral Group and its Automorphism Group
nodes.statement_short: The Coxeter diagram automorphism is $(n-1)x+(n-1)$: outer for even $n$, inner for odd $n$.
nodes.label: coxeter-example

nodes.name: ZDiv(c)
nodes.statement:
For any $c\in\mathbb{Z}_n$, we define $\zdiv{c}=\{y\in\mathbb{Z}_n\mid cy\equiv 0
\mbox{ mod } n\}$.

nodes.name: ZDiv(c) is a subgroup of order gcd(c,n)
nodes.statement:
It is trivial to check that $\zdiv{c}$ is a
subgroup of $\mathbb{Z}_n$. In particular, $\zdiv{c}=\operatorname{ker}\pi_{c}$ where
$\pi_{c}:\mathbb{Z}_n\to\mathbb{Z}_n$ given by $\pi_{c}(x)=cx$. Note that
$\operatorname{im}(\pi_{c})=\langle c\rangle$ and so
$|\operatorname{im}(\pi_{c})|=\frac{n}{\gcd(c,n)}$. Since $\operatorname{im}(\pi_{c})\cong
\mathbb{Z}_n/\operatorname{ker}(\pi_{c})\cong \mathbb{Z}_n/\zdiv{c}$, it follows that
$|\zdiv{c}|=\gcd(c,n)$.
nodes.statement_short: $\operatorname{ZDiv}(c)$ is the kernel of multiplication by $c$, a subgroup of order $\gcd(c,n)$.

nodes.name: Automorphisms of order dividing k
nodes.statement:
Let $k\geq 1$ be an integer and $\theta\in\operatorname{Aut}(D_n)$ with
$\theta=ax+b$. Then $\theta^k={\sf id}$ if and only if $a\in\mathcal{R}_n^k$ and $b\in \zdiv{a^{k-1}+a^{k-2}+\cdots +a+1}$.
conclusions: $\theta^k={\sf id}$ if and only if $a\in\mathcal{R}_n^k$ and $b\in \zdiv{a^{k-1}+a^{k-2}+\cdots +a+1}$
nodes.statement_short: $(ax+b)^k=\mathrm{id}$ iff $a$ is a $k$-th root of unity and $b$ is killed by $1+a+\cdots+a^{k-1}$.
nodes.label: prop:orderk

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 2.1
nodes.statement:
Straightforward computation in $\operatorname{Aut}(D_n)$ gives us that 
$$\theta^k=a^kx+(a^{k-1}+a^{k-2}+\cdots +a+1)b$$
Since we have identified the identity automorphism with $x \in \operatorname{Aff}(\mathbb{Z}_n)$
the following two equations hold:
\begin{equation} \begin{aligned}
a^k & \equiv 1 \pmod{n} \\
(a^{k-1} + a^{k-2} + \cdots + 1) b & \equiv 0 \pmod{n}.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
In the notation described above, these are evidently equivalent to $a\in\mathcal{R}_n^k$ and\\ 
$b\in~\zdiv{a^{k-1}+a^{k-2}+\cdots +a+1}$.
nodes.statement_short: Compute $\theta^k=a^kx+(a^{k-1}+\cdots+1)b$ and compare with the identity $x$.

nodes.name: Congruences for theta^k = id
nodes.label: congruences

nodes.name: Compute theta^k
nodes.statement:
Straightforward computation in $\operatorname{Aut}(D_n)$ gives us that 
$$\theta^k=a^kx+(a^{k-1}+a^{k-2}+\cdots +a+1)b$$
nodes.statement_short: Compute $\theta^k$ in $\operatorname{Aff}(\mathbb{Z}_n)$.

nodes.name: Compare with identity
nodes.statement_short: Equating with $x$ gives two congruences.

nodes.name: Translate to R_n^k and ZDiv
nodes.statement:
In the notation described above, these are evidently equivalent to $a\in\mathcal{R}_n^k$ and\\ 
$b\in~\zdiv{a^{k-1}+a^{k-2}+\cdots +a+1}$.
nodes.statement_short: The congruences say $a\in\mathcal{R}_n^k$ and $b\in\operatorname{ZDiv}(\cdot)$.

nodes.name: Aut_k(D_n)
nodes.statement: In what follows, we let $\operatorname{Aut}_k(D_n)=\{\theta\in\operatorname{Aut}(D_n) \mid \theta^k={\sf id}\}\subseteq \operatorname{Aut}(D_n)$.

nodes.name: Number of automorphisms of order dividing k
nodes.statement:
For any $n$ and $k\geq 1$, we have
$$|\operatorname{Aut}_k(D_n)|=\sum_{a\in \mathcal{R}_n^k}\gcd(a^{k-1}+a^{k-2}+\cdots+a+1,n).$$
conclusions: $$|\operatorname{Aut}_k(D_n)|=\sum_{a\in \mathcal{R}_n^k}\gcd(a^{k-1}+a^{k-2}+\cdots+a+1,n).$$
nodes.statement_short: $|\operatorname{Aut}_k(D_n)|$ is the sum over $a\in\mathcal{R}_n^k$ of $\gcd(1+a+\cdots+a^{k-1},n)$.
nodes.label: prop:numauts

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 2.2
nodes.statement:
This follows from Proposition \ref{prop:orderk}: for any $a\in\mathcal{R}_n^k$ there are 
$$\abs{\zdiv{a^{k-1}+a^{k-2}+\cdots+1}}=\gcd(a^{k-1}+a^{k-2}+\cdots+1,n)$$ elements $b$ such that
$(a^{k-1}+a^{k-2}+\cdots+1)b\equiv 0$ (mod $n$), and every automorphism $\theta\in\operatorname{Aut}_k(D_n)$ must be of this form.
nodes.statement_short: Count, for each $a\in\mathcal{R}_n^k$, the $\gcd(\cdot,n)$ admissible $b$ given by Proposition 2.1.

nodes.name: Equivalence of automorphisms
nodes.statement:
Let $\theta_1, \theta_2\in\operatorname{Aut}(D_n)$. 
We say that $\theta_1$ is
\textit{equivalent} to $\theta_2$ and write $\theta_1\sim\theta_2$ if
and only if they are conjugate to each other, i.e. if there is
$\sigma\in\operatorname{Aut}(D_n)$ with $\sigma\theta_1\sigma^{-1}=\theta_2$. For any $\theta\in\operatorname{Aut}(D_n)$ we let $\overline{\theta}=\{\sigma\in\operatorname{Aut}(D_n)\mid \theta\sim \sigma\}$ be the equivalence class of $\theta$.
nodes.statement_short: Two automorphisms are equivalent if conjugate by some automorphism; $\overline{\theta}$ is the class of $\theta$.

nodes.name: Equivalence is broad
nodes.statement:
This definition of equivalence is broad (since we allow conjugation by
any automorphism, not just the inner ones), but still useful. In
particular, it simplifies the statement of the following proposition
and it allows us not to worry about the parity of $n$ in several places.

nodes.name: Criterion for equivalence of automorphisms
nodes.statement:
Let $\theta_1=ax+b\in\operatorname{Aut}(D_n)$ and $\theta_2=cx+d\in\operatorname{Aut}(D_n)$. Then
$\theta_1\sim\theta_2$ if and only if $a=c$ and $fb-d\in\langle
a-1\rangle\leq \mathbb{Z}_n$ for some $f\in U_n$.
conclusions:
$\theta_1\sim\theta_2$ if and only if $a=c$ and $fb-d\in\langle
a-1\rangle\leq \mathbb{Z}_n$ for some $f\in U_n$
nodes.statement_short: $ax+b\sim cx+d$ iff $a=c$ and $fb-d\in\langle a-1\rangle$ for some unit $f$.
nodes.label: prop:equivalence

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 2.5
nodes.statement:
Suppose that $\sigma=fx+g\in\operatorname{Aut}(D_n)$ (so that $f\in U_n$ and $g\in\mathbb{Z}_n$). It is easily checked that $\sigma^{-1}=f^{-1}x-f^{-1}g$
  where $f^{-1}\in\mathbb{Z}_n$ since $f\in U_n$. Then
  $\sigma\theta_1\sigma^{-1}=\tau$, where
  $\tau=f(a(f^{-1}x-f^{-1}g)+b)+g=ax+fb-g(a-1)$. Thus, we can conclude
  that $\sigma\theta_1\sigma^{-1}=\theta_2$ if and only if $a=c$ and
  $fb-g(a-1)= d$. The second equation can be written as $fb-d=g(a-1)$, and thus $fb-d\in\langle
  a-1\rangle$.
nodes.statement_short: Compute the conjugate $\sigma\theta_1\sigma^{-1}=ax+fb-g(a-1)$ for $\sigma=fx+g$ and compare coefficients.

nodes.name: Introduce sigma and its inverse
nodes.statement:
Suppose that $\sigma=fx+g\in\operatorname{Aut}(D_n)$ (so that $f\in U_n$ and $g\in\mathbb{Z}_n$). It is easily checked that $\sigma^{-1}=f^{-1}x-f^{-1}g$
  where $f^{-1}\in\mathbb{Z}_n$ since $f\in U_n$.
nodes.statement_short: Take $\sigma=fx+g$ with inverse $f^{-1}x-f^{-1}g$.

nodes.name: Compute the conjugate
nodes.statement:
Then
  $\sigma\theta_1\sigma^{-1}=\tau$, where
  $\tau=f(a(f^{-1}x-f^{-1}g)+b)+g=ax+fb-g(a-1)$.
nodes.statement_short: $\sigma\theta_1\sigma^{-1}=ax+fb-g(a-1)$.

nodes.name: Compare coefficients
nodes.statement:
Thus, we can conclude
  that $\sigma\theta_1\sigma^{-1}=\theta_2$ if and only if $a=c$ and
  $fb-g(a-1)= d$. The second equation can be written as $fb-d=g(a-1)$, and thus $fb-d\in\langle
  a-1\rangle$.
nodes.statement_short: Equality with $\theta_2$ iff $a=c$ and $fb-d\in\langle a-1\rangle$.

nodes.name: Equivalence classes of Aut_k(D_n)
nodes.statement:
Suppose $n$ is fixed and let $k\geq 1$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item
For any $a\in\mathcal{R}_n^k$, $\langle a-1\rangle\leq \zdiv{a^{k-1}+a^{k-2}+\cdots+a+1}$.
\item
For any $a\in\mathcal{R}_n^k$, $U_n$ acts on the cosets $\zdiv{a^{k-1}+a^{k-2}+\cdots+a+1}/\langle a-1\rangle$.
\item
The set $\operatorname{Aut}_k(D_n)$ is partitioned into equivalence classes indexed by pairs $(a,B)$ where $a\in\mathcal{R}_n^k$ and $B$ is an orbit of $U_n$ on \hbox{$\zdiv{a^{k-1}+a^{k-2}+\cdots +a+1}/\langle a-1\rangle$}.
\end{enumerate}
conclusions: For any $a\in\mathcal{R}_n^k$, $\langle a-1\rangle\leq \zdiv{a^{k-1}+a^{k-2}+\cdots+a+1}$.
For any $a\in\mathcal{R}_n^k$, $U_n$ acts on the cosets $\zdiv{a^{k-1}+a^{k-2}+\cdots+a+1}/\langle a-1\rangle$.

The set $\operatorname{Aut}_k(D_n)$ is partitioned into equivalence classes indexed by pairs $(a,B)$ where $a\in\mathcal{R}_n^k$ and $B$ is an orbit of $U_n$ on \hbox{$\zdiv{a^{k-1}+a^{k-2}+\cdots +a+1}/\langle a-1\rangle$}.
nodes.statement_short: Equivalence classes in $\operatorname{Aut}_k(D_n)$ are indexed by $a\in\mathcal{R}_n^k$ and a $U_n$-orbit on $\operatorname{ZDiv}(1+\cdots+a^{k-1})/\langle a-1\rangle$.
nodes.label: lem:equivalence

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 2.6
nodes.statement: Part (1) is trivial since $(a-1)(a^{k-1}+a^{k-2}+\cdots +a+1)=a^k-1\equiv 0$. For part (2), we simply recognize that $U_n=\operatorname{Aut}(\mathbb{Z}_n)$ acts on $\mathbb{Z}_n$ by multiplication and since every subgroup is cyclic, $U_n$ must stabilize the subgroups of $\mathbb{Z}_n$. Finally, part (3) is simply Proposition \ref{prop:equivalence} in terms of the $U_n$-action on $\zdiv{a^{k-1}+a^{k-2}+\cdots +a+1}/\langle a-1\rangle$.
nodes.statement_short: Part by part: $(a-1)(1+\cdots+a^{k-1})=a^k-1$; $U_n$ stabilises subgroups of $\mathbb{Z}_n$; part (3) restates Proposition 2.5.

nodes.name: Part (1)
nodes.statement: Part (1) is trivial since $(a-1)(a^{k-1}+a^{k-2}+\cdots +a+1)=a^k-1\equiv 0$.

nodes.name: Part (2)
nodes.statement: For part (2), we simply recognize that $U_n=\operatorname{Aut}(\mathbb{Z}_n)$ acts on $\mathbb{Z}_n$ by multiplication and since every subgroup is cyclic, $U_n$ must stabilize the subgroups of $\mathbb{Z}_n$.
nodes.statement_short: $U_n=\operatorname{Aut}(\mathbb{Z}_n)$ stabilises every (cyclic) subgroup.

nodes.name: Part (3)
nodes.statement: Finally, part (3) is simply Proposition \ref{prop:equivalence} in terms of the $U_n$-action on $\zdiv{a^{k-1}+a^{k-2}+\cdots +a+1}/\langle a-1\rangle$.
nodes.statement_short: Part (3) is Proposition 2.5 rephrased via the $U_n$-action.

nodes.name: Number N_a of equivalence classes with leading coefficient a
nodes.statement: N_a:=|\{\overline{\theta}\mid \theta=ax+b\in\operatorname{Aut}_k(D_n)\}|.
nodes.label: eq:numequiv

nodes.name: N_a counts U_n-orbits
nodes.statement: According to Proposition \ref{lem:equivalence}, given $a\in\mathcal{R}_n^k$, computing $N_a$ amounts to counting the number of orbits of the $U_n$-action on $\zdiv{a^{k-1}+a^{k-2}+\cdots +a+1}/\langle a-1\rangle$.

nodes.name: Number of U_n-orbits
nodes.statement:
Let $n$ be fixed and let $a\in\mathcal{R}_n^k$. Then, the number of orbits of $U_n$ on $\zdiv{a^{k-1}+a^{k-2}+\cdots +a+1}/\langle a-1\rangle$ is equal to the number of divisors of 
$$\frac{\gcd(a-1,n)\gcd(a^{k-1}+a^{k-2}+\cdots+a+1,n)}{n}.$$
conclusions:
the number of orbits of $U_n$ on $\zdiv{a^{k-1}+a^{k-2}+\cdots +a+1}/\langle a-1\rangle$ is equal to the number of divisors of 
$$\frac{\gcd(a-1,n)\gcd(a^{k-1}+a^{k-2}+\cdots+a+1,n)}{n}.$$
nodes.statement_short: The number of $U_n$-orbits on $\operatorname{ZDiv}(1+\cdots+a^{k-1})/\langle a-1\rangle$ equals the number of divisors of $\gcd(a-1,n)\gcd(1+\cdots+a^{k-1},n)/n$.
nodes.label: unorbits

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 2.7
nodes.statement: The $U_n$-orbits on $\mathbb{Z}_n$ are indexed by the subgroups of $\mathbb{Z}_n$. Thus, the $U_n$-orbits on $\zdiv{a^{k-1}+a^{k-2}+\cdots +a+1}/\langle a-1\rangle$ are indexed by subgroups $L\leq \mathbb{Z}_n$ such that $\langle a-1\rangle\leq L\leq \zdiv{a^{k-1}+a^{k-2}+\cdots +a+1}$. It is well known that the subgroup lattice of $\mathbb{Z}_n$ is isomorphic to the divisor lattice of $n$. Under the previous lattice isomorphism, the subgroup $\langle a-1\rangle$ corresponds to the divisor $\gcd(a-1,n)$ and the subgroup $\zdiv{a^{k-1}+a^{k-2}+\cdots +a+1}$ corresponds to the divisor $$\frac{n}{\gcd(a^{k-1}+\cdots+a+1,n)},$$ and the subgroups between these groups correspond to the divisors of $n$ between $\gcd(a-1,n)$ and  $\frac{n}{\gcd(a^{k-1}+\cdots+a+a,n)}$ in the divisor lattice. Finally, it is known that this sub-lattice of the divisors of $n$ is isomorphic to the divisor lattice of $$\frac{\gcd(a-1,n)}{\frac{n}{\gcd(a^{k-1}+\cdots+a+1,n)}}=\frac{\gcd(a-1,n)\gcd(a^{k-1}+a^{k-2}+\cdots+a+1,n)}{n}.$$
nodes.statement_short: Orbits correspond to intermediate subgroups of $\mathbb{Z}_n$, i.e. to an interval of the divisor lattice of $n$, which is the divisor lattice of the quotient.

nodes.name: Orbits as intermediate subgroups
nodes.statement: The $U_n$-orbits on $\mathbb{Z}_n$ are indexed by the subgroups of $\mathbb{Z}_n$. Thus, the $U_n$-orbits on $\zdiv{a^{k-1}+a^{k-2}+\cdots +a+1}/\langle a-1\rangle$ are indexed by subgroups $L\leq \mathbb{Z}_n$ such that $\langle a-1\rangle\leq L\leq \zdiv{a^{k-1}+a^{k-2}+\cdots +a+1}$.
nodes.statement_short: $U_n$-orbits on the quotient correspond to subgroups between $\langle a-1\rangle$ and $\operatorname{ZDiv}$.

nodes.name: Translate to divisor lattice
nodes.statement: It is well known that the subgroup lattice of $\mathbb{Z}_n$ is isomorphic to the divisor lattice of $n$. Under the previous lattice isomorphism, the subgroup $\langle a-1\rangle$ corresponds to the divisor $\gcd(a-1,n)$ and the subgroup $\zdiv{a^{k-1}+a^{k-2}+\cdots +a+1}$ corresponds to the divisor $$\frac{n}{\gcd(a^{k-1}+\cdots+a+1,n)},$$ and the subgroups between these groups correspond to the divisors of $n$ between $\gcd(a-1,n)$ and  $\frac{n}{\gcd(a^{k-1}+\cdots+a+a,n)}$ in the divisor lattice.
nodes.statement_short: Use the subgroup lattice of $\mathbb{Z}_n$ $\cong$ divisor lattice of $n$.

nodes.name: Count divisors
nodes.statement: Finally, it is known that this sub-lattice of the divisors of $n$ is isomorphic to the divisor lattice of $$\frac{\gcd(a-1,n)}{\frac{n}{\gcd(a^{k-1}+\cdots+a+1,n)}}=\frac{\gcd(a-1,n)\gcd(a^{k-1}+a^{k-2}+\cdots+a+1,n)}{n}.$$
nodes.statement_short: The interval is the divisor lattice of the stated quotient.

nodes.name: H_theta and Q_theta
nodes.statement:
Namely, given an
automorphism, $\theta$, we want to compute

$$
\begin{aligned}
H_\theta&=G^\theta=\{x\in G\mid \theta(x)=x\}\ \mbox{and}\\
Q_\theta&=\{g\in G\mid g=x\theta(x)^{-1} \mbox{ for some } x\in G\}.
\end{aligned}$$

When $\theta$ is understood to be fixed, we drop the subscript from
our notation.

nodes.name: Fixed group and symmetric space of an automorphism of D_n
nodes.statement:
Let $G=D_n$ and $\theta=ax+b\in\operatorname{Aut}(D_n)$ be of finite order, and let
$H$ and $Q$ be as defined above. Then
$$
\begin{aligned}
H&=\{r^k\mid k(a-1)\equiv 0 \mbox{ (mod $n$)}\}\cup \{r^ks\mid k(a-1)\equiv -b \mbox{ (mod $n$)}\}\ \mbox{and}\\
Q&=\{r^k\mid k\in\langle a-1\rangle\cup(-b+\langle a-1\rangle)\}.
\end{aligned}
$$
nodes.section: 3 Fixed Groups and Symmetric Spaces of Automorphisms
assumptions:
Let $G=D_n$ and $\theta=ax+b\in\operatorname{Aut}(D_n)$ be of finite order, and let
$H$ and $Q$ be as defined above.
nodes.statement_short: Explicit description of $H$ (rotations and reflections fixed by $ax+b$) and $Q$ (rotations $r^k$ with $k\in\langle a-1\rangle\cup(-b+\langle a-1\rangle)$).
nodes.label: thm:hqr

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 3.1
nodes.statement:
Recall that if $\theta=ax+b\in\operatorname{Aut}(D_n)$, then the formula
  $\theta(r^ks^m)=r^{ak+bm}s^m$ provides the full description of the
  action of $\theta$. All of the results of the theorem arise from the
  definitions of $H$ and $Q$ using the action described above by
  $\theta$. We demonstrate the computation for $H$ in what
  follows, and $Q$ is similar. Suppose $\theta(r^k)=r^k$, then $r^{ak}=r^k$ and so
  $ak-k\equiv 0$ (mod $n$), i.e. $k(a-1)\equiv 0$ (mod $n$). On the
  other hand, if $\theta(r^ks)=r^ks$, then $r^{ak+b}s=r^ks$ and so
  $ak-k+b\equiv 0$ (mod $n$), i.e. $k(a-1)\equiv -b$ (mod $n$).
nodes.section: 3 Fixed Groups and Symmetric Spaces of Automorphisms
nodes.statement_short: Apply $\theta(r^ks^m)=r^{ak+bm}s^m$ to rotations and reflections separately; $Q$ is similar.

nodes.name: Structure of H
nodes.statement:
Let $\theta=ax+b\in\operatorname{Aut}(D_n)$ be of finite order. Then
\begin{enumerate}
\item
If $b\not\in\langle a-1\rangle$, then $H\cong\zdiv{a-1}$ is cyclic.
\item
If $b\in\langle a-1\rangle$, then $H\cong\zdiv{a-1} \rtimes \mathbb{Z}_2$ is dihedral.
\end{enumerate}
nodes.section: 3 Fixed Groups and Symmetric Spaces of Automorphisms
conclusions: If $b\not\in\langle a-1\rangle$, then $H\cong\zdiv{a-1}$ is cyclic.
If $b\in\langle a-1\rangle$, then $H\cong\zdiv{a-1} \rtimes \mathbb{Z}_2$ is dihedral.
nodes.statement_short: $H$ is cyclic $\cong\operatorname{ZDiv}(a-1)$ if $b\notin\langle a-1\rangle$, dihedral otherwise.

nodes.name: When HQ = D_n
nodes.statement:
Let $\theta=ax+b\in\operatorname{Aut}(D_n)$ be a fixed automorphism. If $b\not\in\langle a-1\rangle$, then $HQ\ne D_n$. If $b\in\langle a-1\rangle$, then the following are equivalent
\begin{enumerate}
\item
$HQ=D_n$
\item
$H\cap Q=\{1\}$ in $D_n$, and
\item
$\gcd(a-1,n)$ is relatively prime to $\frac{n}{\gcd(a-1,n)}$.
\end{enumerate}

conclusions: If $b\not\in\langle a-1\rangle$, then $HQ\ne D_n$.
If $b\in\langle a-1\rangle$, then the following are equivalent
nodes.statement_short: $HQ\ne D_n$ if $b\notin\langle a-1\rangle$; otherwise $HQ=D_n$ iff $H\cap Q=1$ iff $\gcd(a-1,n)$ is coprime to $n/\gcd(a-1,n)$.

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 3.4
nodes.statement:
From Corollary \ref{h-structure} and the fact that $Q\subseteq\langle r\rangle$, we see that if $b\not\in\langle a-1\rangle$ then $HQ
\subseteq\langle r\rangle\ne D_n$. If $b\in\langle a-1\rangle$ then $H$ contains a reflection and so $HQ = D_n$ if and only if 
$r\in HQ$. From Corollaries \ref{h-structure} and \ref{cor:qgroup}, we see that $r\in HQ$ if and only if the subgroups 
$\zdiv{a-1}$ and $\langle a-1\rangle$ in $\mathbb{Z}_n$ have relatively prime generators. 
This last condition is clearly equivalent to both (2) and (3).

nodes.name: Three automorphisms of D_36
nodes.statement:
Let $G=D_{36}$. We illustrate Theorem \ref{thm:hqr} and its corollaries for three different 
automorphisms of $D_{36}$. First, consider the automorphism $\theta_1=19x+18$.  Note that $\theta_1$ is an involution. Applying 
Theorem \ref{thm:hqr} yields that for $\theta_1$, $H=H_1=\{1,r^2,r^4,\ldots,r^{34}, r^3s,r^5s,\ldots, r^{35}s\}$ and $Q=Q_1=\{1,r^
{18}\}$, which gives that $H_1\cap Q_1=\{1,r^{18}\}=Q_1$. Observe that the statement of Corollary \ref{cor:qgroup} holds in this 
case: $H_1 Q_1\neq D_{36}$. This follows from the fact that $18\in\langle 18\rangle$, but $\gcd(18,36)=18$ is not relatively prime to 
$36/\gcd(18,36)=2$.  

Now consider $\theta_2=5x+2$ which is an automorphism of order 6. In this case, $H_2=\{1,r^9,r^{18},r^{27}\}$ and $Q_2=
\{1,r^2,r^4,\ldots,r^{34}\}$. Thus, $H_2\cap Q_2=\{1, r^{18}\}$ and $H_2 Q_2=D_{36}$.  However, in this case it is because $2\not\in
\langle 4\rangle$.  

Finally, consider the automorphism $\theta_3 = 5x + 4$ of $D_{36}$. This is also an automorphism of order 6. In this case, $H_3 = 
\{1, r^9, r^{18}, r^{27},  r^8s, r^{17}s, r^{26}s, r^{35}s\}$ and $Q_3 = \{1, r^4, r^8, r^{12}, \ldots , r^{32}\}$. Thus, $H_3 \cap 
Q_3 = \{1\}$ and this agrees with Corollary \ref{cor:qgroup} since $r^9r^{28} = r$ and so $H_3 Q_3 = D_{36}$.
nodes.section: 3 Fixed Groups and Symmetric Spaces of Automorphisms
nodes.statement_short: Computes $H$, $Q$, $H\cap Q$ and $HQ$ for $19x+18$, $5x+2$, $5x+4$ in $D_{36}$.

nodes.name: H-orbits and G-orbits on Q
nodes.statement:
Let $G=D_n$ and $\theta=ax+b\in\operatorname{Aut}_k(D_n)$ for some $k$. 
\begin{enumerate}
\item
If $b\not\in\langle a-1\rangle$, then the $H$-orbits on $Q$ are:
$$H\backslash Q=\left\{\{r^j\}\mid j\in \langle a-1\rangle\cup(-b+\langle a-1\rangle)\right\}.$$
\item
If $b\in\langle a-1\rangle$, then the $H$-orbits on $Q$ are:
$$H\backslash Q=\left\{\{r^j, r^{-j}\}\mid j\in \langle a-1\rangle\right\}.$$
\end{enumerate}
In either situation $G\backslash Q=\{Q\}$, i.e. there is a single $G$-orbit on $Q$.

conclusions:

$$H\backslash Q=\left\{\{r^j\}\mid j\in \langle a-1\rangle\cup(-b+\langle a-1\rangle)\right\}.$$

If $b\in\langle a-1\rangle$, then the $H$-orbits on $Q$ are:

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 3.6
nodes.statement:
Since $H$ is fixed by $\theta$, the action of $H$ on $Q$ is simply by conjugation. We note that $Q\subseteq \langle r\rangle\leq D_n$ 
and so we only need to describe the action of $H$ on a general element, $r^j$. Then, let $r^i\in\{r^k\mid k(a-1)\equiv 0 \pmod{n}\}
\subseteq H$. We see $r^ir^jr^{-i}=r^j$ so $\langle r\rangle$ fixes $Q$ pointwise. Now suppose $r^is\in\{r^ks\mid k(a-1)\equiv -b
\pmod{n}\}\subseteq H$. We have $r^isr^j(r^is)^{-1}=r^{-j}$ and so $r^is$ takes $r^j$ to $r^{-j}$. The result now follows since we 
will have $\{r^j,r^{-j}\}$ as an orbit if and only if there is $r^is\in H$, which is true if and only if $b\in\langle a-1\rangle$.

Finally, we demonstrate that every element of $Q$ is in the $G$-orbit of $1\in Q$. Notice that every element of $Q$ is either of the 
form $q_1=r^{p(a-1)}\in Q$ or $q_2=r^{-b+p(a-1)}\in Q$. We have $r^{-p}\in G$ and $r^{-p}1\theta(r^{-p})^{-1}=r^{p(a-1)}=q_1$. 
Additionally, we have $r^{-p}s\in G$ and $r^{-p}s1\theta(r^{-p}s)^{-1}=r^{-p}r^{ap-b}=r^{-b+p(a-1)}=q_2$. Therefore, for any $q\in Q
$, we can find $g\in G$ such that $g1\theta(g)^{-1}=q$ and so $G*1=Q$. Hence $G\backslash Q=\{Q\}$.

nodes.statement_short: $H$ acts by conjugation: rotations fix $Q\subseteq\langle r\rangle$ pointwise, reflections invert. Transitivity of $G$ by exhibiting $g$ with $g*1=q$.

nodes.name: Number of square roots of unity mod n
nodes.statement:
Suppose that $n\geq 1$ and $n=2^mp_1^{r_1}\cdots p_k^{r_k}$ where the $p_i$ are distinct odd primes. Then,
$$|\mathcal{R}_n^2|=\begin{cases}
2^k & \mbox{ if $m=0,1$}\\
2^{k+1} & \mbox{ if $m=2$}\\
2^{k+2} & \mbox{ if $m\geq 3$}.
\end{cases}$$
assumptions: $n\geq 1$ and $n=2^mp_1^{r_1}\cdots p_k^{r_k}$ where the $p_i$ are distinct odd primes
conclusions:
$$|\mathcal{R}_n^2|=\begin{cases}
2^k & \mbox{ if $m=0,1$}\\
2^{k+1} & \mbox{ if $m=2$}\\
2^{k+2} & \mbox{ if $m\geq 3$}.
\end{cases}$$
nodes.statement_short: $|\mathcal{R}_n^2|$ is $2^k$, $2^{k+1}$ or $2^{k+2}$ according as $m\le1$, $m=2$, $m\ge3$.

nodes.name: Constructing square roots of unity
nodes.statement:
We include the proof of Theorem \ref{thm:squareroots1} in Appendix \ref{sec:appendix} because it demonstrates
exactly how to construct the square roots of unity in $\mathbb{Z}_n$ provided we have
the prime factorization of $n$. The construction only involves the 
Euclidean Algorithm and a map provided by the Chinese Remainder
Theorem. One can use the procedure described in the proof to
effectively compute the square roots of unity in $\mathbb{Z}_n$ for any $n$. The construction of the square roots of unity provided in the appendix also provides the understanding necessary for Corollary \ref{cor:equivclassformula} below.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 4.5
nodes.statement:
The first part of (1) is simply a restatement of Proposition \ref{lem:equivalence} part (1). Now, suppose that $|\zdiv{a+1}/\langle a-1\rangle|=j$. It is well known that $|\langle
  a-1\rangle|=\frac{n}{\gcd(a-1,n)}$ and we have already observed that
  $|\zdiv{a+1}|=\gcd(a+1,n)$. Thus we have that
  $\frac{\gcd(a+1,n)}{\frac{n}{\gcd(a-1,n)}}=j$, or
  $\gcd(a+1,n)\gcd(a-1,n)=jn$. Now, suppose that
$$n=2^mp_1^{r_1}\cdots p_k^{r_k}$$ 
with $m\geq 0$, the $p_i$ distinct odd primes, and $r_i\geq 1$. Then, we must have that 
\begin{itemize}
\item[]
$\gcd(a+1,n)=2^{m'}p_1^{s_1}\cdots p_k^{s_k}$ with $m'\leq m$ and $0\leq s_i\leq r_i$ for all $i$, and
\item[]
$\gcd(a-1,n)=2^{m''}p_1^{t_1}\cdots p_k^{t_k}$ with $m''\leq m$ and $0\leq t_i\leq r_i$ for all $i$.
\end{itemize}
Now, we note that for all $i\in\{1,...,k\}$ either $s_i=0$ or
$t_i=0$. Indeed, if $s_i>0$ and $t_i>0$ then $p_i$ divides both $a-1$
and $a+1$ which is impossible (since $p_i>2$). Similarly, either
$m'\leq1$ or $m''\leq1$; otherwise, $2^{\min\{m',m''\}}$ divides $a-1$
and $a+1$ which is impossible.

Since $\gcd(a+1,n)\gcd(a-1,n)=jn$, we have that
$$2^{m'+m''}p_1^{s_1+t_1}\cdots p_k^{s_k+t_k}=j2^mp_1^{r_1}\cdots p_k^{r_k}.$$
Now, since for all $i$ either $t_i=0$ or $s_i=0$, we necessarily have
$s_i+t_i=r_i$. Dividing out, we get $2^{m'+m''}=j2^m$. We also know
that $m'\leq m$ and $m''\leq m$ and since either $m'\leq 1$ or
$m''\leq 1$, we have $m\leq m'+m''\leq m+1$. Dividing out we have
$j=2^{m'+m''-m}$ and so $1\leq j\leq 2$ as required.

Now, according to Theorem \ref{unorbits}, $N_a$ is the number of divisors of $\frac{\gcd(a-1,n)\gcd(a+1,n)}{n}$, and thus $N_a$ is the number of divisors of $j$ computed above. Therefore, $N_a=1$ if $j=1$ and $N_a=2$ if $j=2$. In either case, $N_a = |\zdiv{a+1}/\langle a-1 \rangle| \le 2$ proving Claim (2).

Finally, according to the proof of (1), we have $j=2$ if and only if
$m'=1$ and $m''=m$ or $m'=m$ and $m''=1$. In the first case, we have
that $2^m$ divides $a-1$, and in the second case we have that $2^m$
divides $a+1$. Therefore, $a \equiv \pm 1 \pmod{2^m}$.
nodes.statement_short: Write $\gcd(a+1,n)\gcd(a-1,n)=jn$ and compare prime factorisations, using that $a\pm1$ share no odd prime and at most one factor 2. Then $j\in\{1,2\}$, and Theorem 2.7 gives $N_a$ as the number of divisors of $j$.

nodes.name: Part (1) inclusion
nodes.statement: The first part of (1) is simply a restatement of Proposition \ref{lem:equivalence} part (1).
nodes.statement_short: The inclusion is Proposition 2.6(1).

nodes.name: Index j
nodes.statement:
Now, suppose that $|\zdiv{a+1}/\langle a-1\rangle|=j$. It is well known that $|\langle
  a-1\rangle|=\frac{n}{\gcd(a-1,n)}$ and we have already observed that
  $|\zdiv{a+1}|=\gcd(a+1,n)$. Thus we have that
  $\frac{\gcd(a+1,n)}{\frac{n}{\gcd(a-1,n)}}=j$, or
  $\gcd(a+1,n)\gcd(a-1,n)=jn$.
nodes.statement_short: Let $j$ be the index; then $\gcd(a+1,n)\gcd(a-1,n)=jn$.

nodes.name: Factor n and the gcds
nodes.statement:
Now, suppose that
$$n=2^mp_1^{r_1}\cdots p_k^{r_k}$$ 
with $m\geq 0$, the $p_i$ distinct odd primes, and $r_i\geq 1$. Then, we must have that 
\begin{itemize}
\item[]
$\gcd(a+1,n)=2^{m'}p_1^{s_1}\cdots p_k^{s_k}$ with $m'\leq m$ and $0\leq s_i\leq r_i$ for all $i$, and
\item[]
$\gcd(a-1,n)=2^{m''}p_1^{t_1}\cdots p_k^{t_k}$ with $m''\leq m$ and $0\leq t_i\leq r_i$ for all $i$.
\end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: Write $n$ and the two gcds in prime factorised form.

nodes.name: gcd(a+1,n)
nodes.statement:
[]
$\gcd(a+1,n)=2^{m'}p_1^{s_1}\cdots p_k^{s_k}$ with $m'\leq m$ and $0\leq s_i\leq r_i$ for all $i$, and
nodes.statement_short: Factorisation of $\gcd(a+1,n)$.

nodes.name: gcd(a-1,n)
nodes.statement:
[]
$\gcd(a-1,n)=2^{m''}p_1^{t_1}\cdots p_k^{t_k}$ with $m''\leq m$ and $0\leq t_i\leq r_i$ for all $i$.
nodes.statement_short: Factorisation of $\gcd(a-1,n)$.

nodes.name: Disjoint prime support
nodes.statement:
Now, we note that for all $i\in\{1,...,k\}$ either $s_i=0$ or
$t_i=0$. Indeed, if $s_i>0$ and $t_i>0$ then $p_i$ divides both $a-1$
and $a+1$ which is impossible (since $p_i>2$). Similarly, either
$m'\leq1$ or $m''\leq1$; otherwise, $2^{\min\{m',m''\}}$ divides $a-1$
and $a+1$ which is impossible.
nodes.statement_short: $a\pm1$ share no odd prime, and one has 2-adic valuation $\le1$.

nodes.name: j is 1 or 2
nodes.statement:
Since $\gcd(a+1,n)\gcd(a-1,n)=jn$, we have that
$$2^{m'+m''}p_1^{s_1+t_1}\cdots p_k^{s_k+t_k}=j2^mp_1^{r_1}\cdots p_k^{r_k}.$$
Now, since for all $i$ either $t_i=0$ or $s_i=0$, we necessarily have
$s_i+t_i=r_i$. Dividing out, we get $2^{m'+m''}=j2^m$. We also know
that $m'\leq m$ and $m''\leq m$ and since either $m'\leq 1$ or
$m''\leq 1$, we have $m\leq m'+m''\leq m+1$. Dividing out we have
$j=2^{m'+m''-m}$ and so $1\leq j\leq 2$ as required.
nodes.statement_short: Comparing exponents gives $j=2^{m'+m''-m}\in\{1,2\}$.

nodes.name: N_a via Theorem 2.7
nodes.statement: Now, according to Theorem \ref{unorbits}, $N_a$ is the number of divisors of $\frac{\gcd(a-1,n)\gcd(a+1,n)}{n}$, and thus $N_a$ is the number of divisors of $j$ computed above. Therefore, $N_a=1$ if $j=1$ and $N_a=2$ if $j=2$. In either case, $N_a = |\zdiv{a+1}/\langle a-1 \rangle| \le 2$ proving Claim (2).
nodes.statement_short: $N_a$ is the number of divisors of $j$, so $N_a=j$.

nodes.name: Condition for N_a = 2
nodes.statement:
Finally, according to the proof of (1), we have $j=2$ if and only if
$m'=1$ and $m''=m$ or $m'=m$ and $m''=1$. In the first case, we have
that $2^m$ divides $a-1$, and in the second case we have that $2^m$
divides $a+1$. Therefore, $a \equiv \pm 1 \pmod{2^m}$.
nodes.statement_short: $j=2$ iff $2^m$ divides $a-1$ or $a+1$.

nodes.name: Closed formula for the number of equivalence classes of involutions
nodes.statement:
Suppose that $n\geq 1$ and $n=2^mp_1^{r_1}\cdots p_k^{r_k}$ where the $p_i$ are distinct odd primes. Then, the number of equivalence classes, $C_n$, of $\operatorname{Aut}_2(D_n)$ is given by
$$C_n=\begin{cases}
2^k & \mbox{ if $m=0$}\\
2^{k+1} & \mbox{ if $m=1$}\\
2^{k+2} & \mbox{ if $m=2$}\\
2^{k+3}-2^{k+1} & \mbox{ if $m\geq 3$}.
\end{cases}$$
assumptions: $n\geq 1$ and $n=2^mp_1^{r_1}\cdots p_k^{r_k}$ where the $p_i$ are distinct odd primes
conclusions:
the number of equivalence classes, $C_n$, of $\operatorname{Aut}_2(D_n)$ is given by
$$C_n=\begin{cases}
2^k & \mbox{ if $m=0$}\\
2^{k+1} & \mbox{ if $m=1$}\\
2^{k+2} & \mbox{ if $m=2$}\\
2^{k+3}-2^{k+1} & \mbox{ if $m\geq 3$}.
\end{cases}$$
nodes.label: cor:equivclassformula

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 4.6
nodes.statement: According to Theorem \ref{thm:equivinvols}, we know $N_a$ for every $a\in\mathcal{R}_n^2$. When $m=0$, $n$ is odd and we know that $N_a=1$ for all $a$. Thus, there is one equivalence class for every element of $\mathcal{R}_n^2$ proving the first formula. If $m=1,2$, then every $a\in\mathcal{R}_n^2$ is odd and so satisfies $a\equiv \pm 1\pmod{m}$. Thus for every element $a\in\mathcal{R}_n^2$, we get two equivalence classes for a total of $2\cdot|\mathcal{R}_n^2|$ equivalence classes. Finally, when $m\geq 3$, using the construction of the elements of $\mathcal{R}_n^2$ found in the proof in the appendix, we see that exactly half of these elements satisfy the condition $a\equiv\pm 1\pmod{m}$. Therefore, for half the elements in $\mathcal{R}_n^2$ we have $N_a=1$ and for the other half we have $N_a=2$ giving us a total of $2^{k+2}+(2^{k+2}-\frac{1}{2}\cdot2^{k+2})=2^{k+3}-2^{k+1}$ equivalence classes, proving the result.
nodes.statement_short: Case analysis on the 2-adic valuation $m$, summing $N_a$ from Theorem 4.5 over $\mathcal{R}_n^2$.

nodes.name: N_a known
nodes.statement: According to Theorem \ref{thm:equivinvols}, we know $N_a$ for every $a\in\mathcal{R}_n^2$.
nodes.statement_short: Theorem 4.5 gives every $N_a$.

nodes.name: m = 0
nodes.statement: When $m=0$, $n$ is odd and we know that $N_a=1$ for all $a$. Thus, there is one equivalence class for every element of $\mathcal{R}_n^2$ proving the first formula.
nodes.statement_short: Odd $n$: one class per $a$.

nodes.name: m = 1,2
nodes.statement: If $m=1,2$, then every $a\in\mathcal{R}_n^2$ is odd and so satisfies $a\equiv \pm 1\pmod{m}$. Thus for every element $a\in\mathcal{R}_n^2$, we get two equivalence classes for a total of $2\cdot|\mathcal{R}_n^2|$ equivalence classes.
nodes.statement_short: Each $a$ gives two classes.

nodes.name: m >= 3
nodes.statement: Finally, when $m\geq 3$, using the construction of the elements of $\mathcal{R}_n^2$ found in the proof in the appendix, we see that exactly half of these elements satisfy the condition $a\equiv\pm 1\pmod{m}$. Therefore, for half the elements in $\mathcal{R}_n^2$ we have $N_a=1$ and for the other half we have $N_a=2$ giving us a total of $2^{k+2}+(2^{k+2}-\frac{1}{2}\cdot2^{k+2})=2^{k+3}-2^{k+1}$ equivalence classes, proving the result.
nodes.statement_short: Half the $a$ give two classes.

nodes.name: OEIS connection with group extensions
nodes.statement: According to the Online Encyclopedia of Integer Sequences, the sequence described in Corollary \ref{cor:equivclassformula} also counts the number (up to isomorphism) of groups of order $2n$ that have a subgroup isomorphic to $\mathbb Z_n$ \cite{oeisA147848}. To be more precise, we include a brief discussion of the natural bijection between these two objects. Suppose $\theta=ax+b$ is an involution. Then $w_a:\mathbb{Z}_2\to\operatorname{Aut}(\mathbb{Z}_n)=U_n$ given by $w_a(0)=1$ and $w_a(1)=-a$ is an injective homomorphism and induces a $\mathbb{Z}_2$-action on $\mathbb{Z}_n$. Next, we define $f:\mathbb{Z}_2\times\mathbb{Z}_2\to\mathbb{Z}_n$ by $f(c,d)=0$ if $c=0$ or $d=0$ and $f(1,1)=b$; it is easily shown that $f$ is a 2-cocycle if and only if $b\in\zdiv{a+1}$. Finally, it is well known (see \cite[Chapter 6.6]{weibel})) that 2-cocyles give rise to group extensions and two different 2-cocycles give isomorphic group extensions if they are cohomologous. A simple calculation shows that if $\theta=ax+b$ and $\theta'=ax+b'$, then the corresponding 2-cocycles are cohomologous if and only if $b-b'\in\langle a-1\rangle$, which matches the characterization of automorphisms being equivalent above.
nodes.statement_short: $C_n$ also counts groups of order $2n$ with a subgroup $\cong\mathbb{Z}_n$, via 2-cocycles $f(1,1)=b$ for the action $w_a$.

nodes.name: Twisted involutions R
nodes.statement:
We now use our previous results from Section \ref{sec:results-aut} to
fully describe the sets $H_\theta$ and $Q_\theta$ when $\theta$ is an 
involution; moreover, in this situation, we are also interested in the set of twisted involutions
$$R=R_\theta=\{x\in G\mid \theta(x)=x^{-1}\}.$$

nodes.name: Twisted involutions of an involution of D_n
nodes.statement: R=\{r^k\mid k\in\zdiv{a+1}\}\cup \{r^ks\mid k(a-1)\equiv -b\pmod{n}\}.
nodes.label: eqn:R

nodes.name: Q is a subgroup for involutions
nodes.statement:
If $\theta=ax+b$ is an involution, then $Q$ is a subgroup of $\langle
r \rangle$ and under the natural isomorphism $\psi: \langle r \rangle
\buildrel\cong\over\longrightarrow \mathbb{Z}_n$ we have 
\[ \psi(Q) = \begin{cases}
\langle a-1 \rangle, & \text{if} \quad b \in \langle a-1 \rangle \\
\zdiv{a+1}, & \text{otherwise.}
\end{cases} \]
Furthermore, 
$R \setminus Q = \{r^k\mid k\in\zdiv{a+1}\setminus\langle a-1\rangle\}\cup\{r^ks \mid k(a-1)\equiv -b\pmod{n}\}$
conclusions:
$Q$ is a subgroup of $\langle
r \rangle$
$R \setminus Q = \{r^k\mid k\in\zdiv{a+1}\setminus\langle a-1\rangle\}\cup\{r^ks \mid k(a-1)\equiv -b\pmod{n}\}$
nodes.statement_short: For an involution, $Q$ is a cyclic subgroup of rotations, $\langle a-1\rangle$ or $\operatorname{ZDiv}(a+1)$, and $R\setminus Q$ is explicit.
nodes.label: cor:Q-is-ZDiv

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 4.8
nodes.statement:
We proceed using Theorem \ref{thm:hqr} and
  applying Theorem \ref{thm:equivinvols}. Indeed, by Theorem \ref{thm:hqr} $\psi(Q)$ consists of the
  union of the two cosets $\langle a-1 \rangle$ and $-b + \langle a-1
  \rangle$. These cosets are
  the same if $-b \in \langle a-1 \rangle$ (which means $b\in\langle a-1\rangle$) and then $\psi(Q) = \langle a - 1 \rangle \le \zdiv{a+1}$, or they are
  distinct and by Theorem \ref{thm:equivinvols} part (1) there are
  only 2 cosets total so 
  $\langle a - 1 \rangle \cup (-b+\langle a - 1 \rangle) =
  \zdiv{a+1}$. In either case, $Q$ is a subgroup of $\langle r
  \rangle$ and $\psi(Q)$ is as described in the statement of the
  corollary. Finally, the result about $R \setminus Q$ is immediate
  from equation \eqref{eqn:R}.
nodes.statement_short: $\psi(Q)$ is the union of two cosets of $\langle a-1\rangle$, equal or filling $\operatorname{ZDiv}(a+1)$ by Theorem 4.5(1).

nodes.name: Two cosets
nodes.statement:
We proceed using Theorem \ref{thm:hqr} and
  applying Theorem \ref{thm:equivinvols}. Indeed, by Theorem \ref{thm:hqr} $\psi(Q)$ consists of the
  union of the two cosets $\langle a-1 \rangle$ and $-b + \langle a-1
  \rangle$.
nodes.statement_short: By Theorem 3.1, $\psi(Q)$ is a union of two cosets.

nodes.name: Cosets equal or fill ZDiv
nodes.statement:
These cosets are
  the same if $-b \in \langle a-1 \rangle$ (which means $b\in\langle a-1\rangle$) and then $\psi(Q) = \langle a - 1 \rangle \le \zdiv{a+1}$, or they are
  distinct and by Theorem \ref{thm:equivinvols} part (1) there are
  only 2 cosets total so 
  $\langle a - 1 \rangle \cup (-b+\langle a - 1 \rangle) =
  \zdiv{a+1}$.
nodes.statement_short: Either the cosets coincide or, by index 2, they fill $\operatorname{ZDiv}(a+1)$.

nodes.name: Q subgroup
nodes.statement:
In either case, $Q$ is a subgroup of $\langle r
  \rangle$ and $\psi(Q)$ is as described in the statement of the
  corollary.
nodes.statement_short: Hence $Q$ is a subgroup as described.

nodes.name: R minus Q
nodes.statement:
Finally, the result about $R \setminus Q$ is immediate
  from equation \eqref{eqn:R}.
nodes.statement_short: Read off $R\setminus Q$ from (4.1).

nodes.name: R = Q when b not in <a-1>
nodes.statement: If $b\not\in\langle a-1\rangle$ then $R=Q$.
conclusions: $R=Q$

nodes.name: psi(Q) is almost always ZDiv(a+1)
nodes.statement: We note that due to Theorem \ref{thm:equivinvols}, $\psi(Q)$ given in Corollary \ref{cor:Q-is-ZDiv} is almost always $\zdiv{a+1}$ for involutions. The only instance where $\psi(Q)\ne \zdiv{a+1}$ occurs when $|\zdiv{a+1}/\langle a-1 \rangle|=2$ and $b\in\langle a-1\rangle$.  We revisit $\theta_1=19x+18$ from Example \ref{autexamples}, which is an involution, noting that this is in fact a case where $b\in\langle a-1\rangle$.  Recalling that $Q_1=\{1,r^{18}\}$, we see that $\psi (Q_1)$ is indeed isomorphic to $\langle a-1\rangle=\langle 18\rangle < \mathbb Z_{36}$.  We also have that $R=R_1=\{1,r,r^3,r^5,\dots,r^{17},r^{18},r^{19},r^{21},\dots, r^{35}\}$, and thus $R_1\setminus Q_1=\{r,r^3,r^5,\dots,r^{35}\}$.
nodes.statement_short: $\psi(Q)\ne\operatorname{ZDiv}(a+1)$ only when the index is 2 and $b\in\langle a-1\rangle$; illustrated by $19x+18$ in $D_{36}$.

nodes.name: Helminck-Wang: involutions equivalent iff fixed groups isomorphic
nodes.statement:
In the setting of algebraic groups, it is known that involutions 
$\theta_1 \sim \theta_2$ if and only if $H_{\theta_1}\cong
H_{\theta_2}$ (see \cite{Helm-Wang93}).
assumptions: In the setting of algebraic groups
conclusions:
involutions 
$\theta_1 \sim \theta_2$ if and only if $H_{\theta_1}\cong
H_{\theta_2}$

nodes.name: Equal fixed groups need not imply equivalence
nodes.statement:
There exists $n$ and involutions $\theta_1,\theta_2\in\operatorname{Aut}(D_n)$
  such that $H_{\theta_1} = H_{\theta_2}$ but
  $\theta_1 \not\sim \theta_2$.
conclusions:
There exists $n$ and involutions $\theta_1,\theta_2\in\operatorname{Aut}(D_n)$
  such that $H_{\theta_1} = H_{\theta_2}$ but
  $\theta_1 \not\sim \theta_2$.

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 4.11
nodes.statement:
Let $n=8$ and $\theta_1=7x$ and $\theta_2=3x$. According to
  Proposition \ref{prop:equivalence}, $\theta_1\not\sim\theta_2$ because
  $7 \ne 3$ (in $U_8$). However, according to Theorem \ref{thm:hqr},
  $H_{\theta_1}=\{1, r^4, s, r^4s\}$ and $H_{\theta_2}=\{1, r^4, s,
  r^4s\}$.
nodes.statement_short: Counterexample $n=8$, $7x$ and $3x$: inequivalent by Proposition 2.5 but with equal $H$ by Theorem 3.1.

nodes.name: Choose involutions
nodes.statement:
Let $n=8$ and $\theta_1=7x$ and $\theta_2=3x$. According to
  Proposition \ref{prop:equivalence}, $\theta_1\not\sim\theta_2$ because
  $7 \ne 3$ (in $U_8$).
nodes.statement_short: Take $7x$, $3x$ in $D_8$; inequivalent since $7\ne3$.

nodes.name: Equal fixed groups
nodes.statement:
However, according to Theorem \ref{thm:hqr},
  $H_{\theta_1}=\{1, r^4, s, r^4s\}$ and $H_{\theta_2}=\{1, r^4, s,
  r^4s\}$.
nodes.statement_short: Theorem 3.1 gives the same $H$ for both.

nodes.name: Infinite dihedral group
nodes.statement:
However, it turns out that there are similar 
results for the infinite dihedral group
\[ D_\infty=\langle r,s\mid s^2=1,\ rs=sr^{-1}\rangle. \]

nodes.name: Automorphisms of D_infinity
nodes.statement:
In this
case, the automorphisms are the affine linear transformations of $\mathbb{Z}$,
so are of the form $ax+b$ where $b\in\mathbb{Z}$ and $a\in\{\pm 1\}$.
conclusions:
the automorphisms are the affine linear transformations of $\mathbb{Z}$,
so are of the form $ax+b$ where $b\in\mathbb{Z}$ and $a\in\{\pm 1\}$

nodes.name: Finite-order automorphisms of D_infinity
conclusions:
If $\theta \in \operatorname{Aut}(D_\infty)$ has finite order, 
then $\theta = -x + b$ for some integer $b$.
$-x + b \sim -x + d$ if and only if $b \equiv d \pmod{2}$.
nodes.label: prop:D-infnity-invol

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 5.1
nodes.statement:
Part (1) follows from the equations \eqref{congruences} given in the proof of Proposition
\ref{prop:orderk}. For part (2), observe that Proposition
\ref{prop:equivalence} holds for $D_\infty$ and says that 
$-x + b \sim -x + d$ if and only if either $b - d \in 2\mathbb{Z}$ or $-b-d
\in 2\mathbb{Z}$, equivalently: $b \equiv d \pmod{2}$.
nodes.statement_short: Solve the congruences (2.1) over $\mathbb{Z}$; apply Proposition 2.5 with $a=-1$.

nodes.name: Two classes of involutions of D_infinity
nodes.statement:
We see that in $D_\infty$ the situation is simple: the only automorphisms
of finite order are involutions and there are only two distinct
equivalence classes of involutions represented by $\chi_0 = -x = \operatorname{conj}(s)$
(inner) and $\chi_1 = -x+1$ (outer).
conclusions:
the only automorphisms
of finite order are involutions and there are only two distinct
equivalence classes of involutions represented by $\chi_0 = -x = \operatorname{conj}(s)$
(inner) and $\chi_1 = -x+1$ (outer)

nodes.name: H, Q, R for involutions of D_infinity
nodes.label: eq:hqr-infty

nodes.name: Corollary 4.8 holds for D_infinity
nodes.statement: We note that the descriptions in equation \eqref{eq:hqr-infty} show that Corollary \ref{cor:Q-is-ZDiv} holds in the infinite case as well. However, in this case, the description is simpler because the description of $Q$ depends only on whether $b$ is even or odd. We also note that despite the fact that the two cases are different when viewing $Q$ as a subgroup of $D_\infty$, we always have $Q\cong \mathbb{Z}$.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 4.1
nodes.statement:
Our goal is to determine the size of $|\mathcal{R}_n^2|$ for all $n$. First, suppose that $n=p^r$ where $p$ is an odd prime and $r\geq
  1$. Then, suppose $a\in\mathbb{Z}_{p^r}$ and that $a^2-1\equiv 0\pmod{p^r}$. Then
  we have that $(a+1)(a-1)\equiv 0$ (mod $p^r$) and so
  $(a+1)(a-1)=kp^r$ for some $k\in\mathbb{Z}$. Since $p$ is an odd prime, it
  is clear that both $a+1$ and $a-1$ cannot divide $p^d$ for any
  $d\geq 1$ and so we have that $a+1=p^r$ or $a-1=p^r$. This implies
  that $a=1$ or $a=n-1$, thus $|\mathcal{R}_{p^r}^2|=2$.  Next, it is
  clear that $|\mathcal{R}_2^2|=1$ and $|\mathcal{R}_4^2|=2$. Suppose that $n=2^m$ with $m\geq 3$. Next, suppose that
  $a\in\mathbb{Z}_n\setminus\{1,n-1\}$ with $a^2\equiv 1$ (mod $n$). Since $n$
  is even, we must have that $a$ is odd, so assume that $a=2k+1$ for
  some $0\leq k\leq 2^{m-1}$. Then $1\equiv a^2\equiv (2k+1)^2\equiv
  4k^2+4k+1$ (mod $n$) so that $4k(k+1)=l\cdot 2^m$ for some $l\geq
  1$. In particular, since $m\geq 3$, we have $k(k+1)=l\cdot 2^{m-2}$
  for some $m$. Either $k$ or $k+1$ is odd and thus cannot divide
  $2^{m-2}$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[] Case 1: $k$ is even. So $k=h\cdot 2^{m-2}$ for some $1\leq
  h\leq 2$ (since $k\leq 2^{m-1})$. Then, if $h=1$, $a=2^{m-1}+1$. If
  $h=2$, then $a\equiv 1$ (mod $n$).
 
\item[] Case 2: $k$ is odd. So $k+1$ is even and $k+1=h\cdot 2^{m-2}$
  with $1\leq h\leq 2$. Then, if $h=1$, $a=2^{m-1}-1$. If $h=2$, then
  $a=2^m-1\equiv n-1\equiv -1$ (mod $n$).
\end{enumerate}

So, there are four possibilities for $a$:
$1,-1,2^{m-1}+1,2^{m-1}-1$. It is easy to check that these are all in
fact square roots of 1, showing that $|\mathcal{R}_{2^m}^2|=4$ if $m\geq 3$.

Finally, the result holds due to the fact that the Chinese Remainder
Theorem guarantees that if $n=2^mp_1^{r_1}\cdots p_k^{r_k}$ then
$$\mathbb{Z}_n\cong \mathbb{Z}_{2^m}\times\mathbb{Z}_{p_1^{r_1}}\times\cdots\times \mathbb{Z}_{p_k^{r_k}}.$$
Then, it is clear that any square root of $(1,...,1)$ (the identity
from the right hand side) must be of the form $(a_0,a_1,...,a_k)$
where $a_0\in\mathcal{R}_{2^m}^2$ and $a_i\in\mathcal{R}_{p_i^{r_i}}^n$ for $i\in\{1,...,k\}$. We have counted the possibilities for $a_i$ above and so we can multiply these
together to get all the possible choices for $a\in\mathbb{Z}_n$ with
$a^2\equiv 1$ (mod $n$). In particular, we get $|\mathcal{R}_n^2|=2^k$ if $m\in\{0,1\}$, $|\mathcal{R}_n^2|=2\cdot2^k$ if $m=2$ and $|\mathcal{R}_n^2|=2^2\cdot2^k$ if $m\geq 3$ as required.
nodes.statement_short: Count square roots of 1 modulo odd prime powers (2) and powers of 2 (1, 2 or 4), then combine by the Chinese Remainder Theorem. Key step: for $2^m$, $m\ge3$, $k(k+1)=l2^{m-2}$ forces $a\in\{\pm1,2^{m-1}\pm1\}$.

nodes.name: Odd prime powers and small powers of 2
nodes.statement:
Our goal is to determine the size of $|\mathcal{R}_n^2|$ for all $n$. First, suppose that $n=p^r$ where $p$ is an odd prime and $r\geq
  1$. Then, suppose $a\in\mathbb{Z}_{p^r}$ and that $a^2-1\equiv 0\pmod{p^r}$. Then
  we have that $(a+1)(a-1)\equiv 0$ (mod $p^r$) and so
  $(a+1)(a-1)=kp^r$ for some $k\in\mathbb{Z}$. Since $p$ is an odd prime, it
  is clear that both $a+1$ and $a-1$ cannot divide $p^d$ for any
  $d\geq 1$ and so we have that $a+1=p^r$ or $a-1=p^r$. This implies
  that $a=1$ or $a=n-1$, thus $|\mathcal{R}_{p^r}^2|=2$.  Next, it is
  clear that $|\mathcal{R}_2^2|=1$ and $|\mathcal{R}_4^2|=2$.
nodes.statement_short: Modulo $p^r$ only $\pm1$; $|\mathcal{R}_2^2|=1$, $|\mathcal{R}_4^2|=2$.

nodes.name: Powers of 2 with m >= 3
nodes.statement:
Suppose that $n=2^m$ with $m\geq 3$. Next, suppose that
  $a\in\mathbb{Z}_n\setminus\{1,n-1\}$ with $a^2\equiv 1$ (mod $n$). Since $n$
  is even, we must have that $a$ is odd, so assume that $a=2k+1$ for
  some $0\leq k\leq 2^{m-1}$. Then $1\equiv a^2\equiv (2k+1)^2\equiv
  4k^2+4k+1$ (mod $n$) so that $4k(k+1)=l\cdot 2^m$ for some $l\geq
  1$. In particular, since $m\geq 3$, we have $k(k+1)=l\cdot 2^{m-2}$
  for some $m$. Either $k$ or $k+1$ is odd and thus cannot divide
  $2^{m-2}$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[] Case 1: $k$ is even. So $k=h\cdot 2^{m-2}$ for some $1\leq
  h\leq 2$ (since $k\leq 2^{m-1})$. Then, if $h=1$, $a=2^{m-1}+1$. If
  $h=2$, then $a\equiv 1$ (mod $n$).
 
\item[] Case 2: $k$ is odd. So $k+1$ is even and $k+1=h\cdot 2^{m-2}$
  with $1\leq h\leq 2$. Then, if $h=1$, $a=2^{m-1}-1$. If $h=2$, then
  $a=2^m-1\equiv n-1\equiv -1$ (mod $n$).
\end{enumerate}

So, there are four possibilities for $a$:
$1,-1,2^{m-1}+1,2^{m-1}-1$. It is easy to check that these are all in
fact square roots of 1, showing that $|\mathcal{R}_{2^m}^2|=4$ if $m\geq 3$.
nodes.statement_short: Analyse $a=2k+1$ with $k(k+1)=l2^{m-2}$: exactly four square roots modulo $2^m$.

nodes.name: Reduce to k(k+1)
nodes.statement:
Suppose that $n=2^m$ with $m\geq 3$. Next, suppose that
  $a\in\mathbb{Z}_n\setminus\{1,n-1\}$ with $a^2\equiv 1$ (mod $n$). Since $n$

nodes.statement_short: Write $a=2k+1$; get $k(k+1)=l2^{m-2}$.

nodes.statement:
[] Case 1: $k$ is even. So $k=h\cdot 2^{m-2}$ for some $1\leq
  h\leq 2$ (since $k\leq 2^{m-1})$. Then, if $h=1$, $a=2^{m-1}+1$. If

[] Case 2: $k$ is odd. So $k+1$ is even and $k+1=h\cdot 2^{m-2}$

nodes.name: Chinese Remainder Theorem
nodes.statement:
Finally, the result holds due to the fact that the Chinese Remainder
Theorem guarantees that if $n=2^mp_1^{r_1}\cdots p_k^{r_k}$ then
$$\mathbb{Z}_n\cong \mathbb{Z}_{2^m}\times\mathbb{Z}_{p_1^{r_1}}\times\cdots\times \mathbb{Z}_{p_k^{r_k}}.$$
Then, it is clear that any square root of $(1,...,1)$ (the identity
from the right hand side) must be of the form $(a_0,a_1,...,a_k)$
where $a_0\in\mathcal{R}_{2^m}^2$ and $a_i\in\mathcal{R}_{p_i^{r_i}}^n$ for $i\in\{1,...,k\}$. We have counted the possibilities for $a_i$ above and so we can multiply these
together to get all the possible choices for $a\in\mathbb{Z}_n$ with
$a^2\equiv 1$ (mod $n$). In particular, we get $|\mathcal{R}_n^2|=2^k$ if $m\in\{0,1\}$, $|\mathcal{R}_n^2|=2\cdot2^k$ if $m=2$ and $|\mathcal{R}_n^2|=2^2\cdot2^k$ if $m\geq 3$ as required.
nodes.statement_short: Multiply the local counts via CRT.
